sources.title: Players on Steam so far seem delighted with Modern Warfare 4's campaign, making it one of the most well-received Call of Dutys in recent history
sources.text: It may be hard to believe, given all the Call of Duty: Modern 4 pre-launch community drama and the beta's lower-than-expected numbers on PC , but the final game may have turned things around - so far, at least. On Steam, Infinity Ward 's final chapter in the Modern Warfare sub-series currently has a Very Positive (92 percent) rating based on over 3,100 user reviews . Modern Warfare 4's campaign early access went live Friday, and the review rating has been improving steadily as players have experienced more of the campaign's missions. Many have likely finished it by now; the campaign is a little over six-hours in length, after all. Gaining access to the campaign on Friday required pre-ordering any of the game's editions digitally. Modern Warfare 4's official release isn't until 23rd October, which makes it hard to determine the current number of players, because SteamDB , our source for this data, can't reveal numbers without its tracking bot having a copy of the game. Setting aside player numbers, the sentiment around Modern Warfare 4 is considerably more positive at the outset compared to last year's Black Ops 7, currently sitting at Mostly Negative (37 percent) . While review ratings change over time with each major update, Modern Warfare 4 is currently the highest-rated Call of Duty in over a decade. However, it's worth bearing in mind that the people playing the game are likely the series' most keen players, so perhaps they're more lenient towards it. We haven't had a chance to review the game yet, having only received code late last week, but IGN published a COD: Modern Warfare 4 campaign review on Friday, scoring it 8/10. In the rebooted Modern Warfare series, the 2019 Modern Warfare game comes closest in average player sentiment with a Mostly Positive rating (79 percent) . 2022's Modern Warfare 2 is far lower with a Mixed rating (45 percent) . Outside of Infinity Ward's output, Black Ops: Cold War is close at Mostly Positive (79 percent) . Modern Warfare 4's next big moment is the anticipated release of DMZ, the game's extraction shooter mode. Like the campaign, DMZ is available early for pre-orders, unlocking tomorrow, 20th October . Finally, on 23rd October, traditional multiplayer becomes available, which is when we're likely to see a shift in user sentiment, if one is going to happen.

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Modern Warfare 4 campaign launches to 94% positive Steam reviews, way ahead of Black Ops 7
sources.text: The campaign for Call of Duty : Modern Warfare 4 is now available for those who pre-ordered, and PC players in particular seem pretty taken by it. The single-player mode has debuted to a strong rating on Steam, indicating this particular installment could be a big one for the franchise. Although Modern Warfare 4 isn't fully out until this coming Friday, October 23, pre-orders come with early access to the campaign. During the beta, this was relegated to a single mission, but now you can knock out the whole thing if you'd like. You'd think this would be a questionable move by Activision and Infinity Ward , but it might just be quite shrewd. If you go on the game's page on Steam, you can see the rating is currently riding extremely high. At time of writing, Modern Warfare 4 is sitting at Very Positive on Valve 's marketplace, based on 94% of reviews. That's a strong opening for any game, and it's especially good for Call of Duty. We don't have hard data on the first weeks of many individual entries of the long-running FPS, but this definitely outdoes the initial feedback on Black Ops 7 and Modern Warfare 3. You can see charts of their reviews going back to launch weeks, and neither were anywhere close to that amount. Whomever came up with the bold move to simply make the campaign part of the perks for being an early adopter, they were onto something. It helps that apparently Infinity Ward's made a good one, which includes 16 missions spread across several locations around the world. Call of Duty campaigns have tended to be a little forgettable over the last ten years or so, since the multiplayer modes and Warzone took prominence. As someone who loves a good solo FPS, it pleases me to see that Modern Warfare 4 is bucking the trend. You can pre-order now if any kind of FOMO is setting in. sources.title: Cyberpunk 2077 terá atualização gratuita com combate usando duas armas e conteúdo de Edgerunners 2
sources.text: A CD Projekt RED anunciou uma nova atualização gratuita para Cyberpunk 2077 . Chamada de Update 2.5 , a novidade será lançada em 22 de outubro de 2026 e incluirá conteúdos inspirados na segunda temporada de Cyberpunk: Edgerunners , que estreou nesta terça-feira (20) na Netflix. Entre as principais mudanças estão a possibilidade de utilizar duas armas simultaneamente durante os combates e novas opções de personalização dos implantes cibernéticos do protagonista. Inicialmente, a atualização estará disponível para PC, PlayStation 5 e Xbox Series X|S . A versão para Nintendo Switch 2 também receberá o conteúdo, mas em uma data posterior, ainda não divulgada. Uma das principais novidades do patch será a introdução de um estilo de combate que permite utilizar duas armas ao mesmo tempo. A desenvolvedora ainda não detalhou quais categorias de armamentos serão compatíveis com a mecânica ou como ela funcionará durante as partidas. Outra mudança confirmada envolve os implantes cibernéticos, que receberão novas possibilidades de personalização. Entretanto, a CD Projekt RED não informou quais componentes poderão ser modificados nem se as novidades terão impacto direto nos atributos do personagem. A atualização também incluirá itens inspirados em Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 , ampliando a conexão entre o jogo e a animação. Para detalhar o conteúdo, a desenvolvedora realizará uma nova edição do REDstreams na quarta-feira, 21 de outubro, às 12h (horário de Brasília) . Durante a transmissão, a empresa apresentará as principais mudanças do Update 2.5 e divulgará a lista completa de novidades. A expectativa é que o evento esclareça o funcionamento do combate com duas armas, as opções de personalização e os conteúdos relacionados ao anime. A atualização acompanha a estreia de Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 , segunda temporada da animação produzida em parceria com o estúdio japonês Trigger. Os dez episódios chegaram à Netflix em 20 de outubro de 2026. Diferentemente da primeira temporada, a nova produção apresenta uma história independente, com novos personagens envolvidos em uma trama de vingança e redenção em Night City. A direção é de Kai Ikarashi, e a narrativa acompanha personagens que tentam sobreviver aos conflitos da cidade. Ainda não foi divulgado quais elementos específicos da nova temporada estarão presentes em Cyberpunk 2077 . Com o lançamento do Update 2.5, a CD Projekt RED amplia o conteúdo do RPG enquanto aproveita a chegada da nova animação ao catálogo da Netflix. Rachele Victoria é formada em Letras, MBA em Inovação e atua há 10 anos com comunicação e conteúdo gamer. Amazon Prime também é feito para jogadores! stories.title: Final Fantasy Resonance review: "A breezy nostalgia-laced JRPG that gives the HD-2D style a shot in the arm"
stories.summary: A defunct gacha mobile game is reborn into a classic but modern adventure

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Final Fantasy Resonance review: "A breezy nostalgia-laced JRPG that gives the HD-2D style a shot in the arm"
sources.text: Like Octopath Traveler 0, Final Fantasy Resonance is a rejuvenated way to experience a story once bound and lost to mobile. It may not reinvent the series, but in giving the HD-2D style a much needed upgrade this retro-modern refresh feels like a mainline adventure in its own right. Engaging battles that mix classic and modern Final Fantasy conventions Generous cadence of side quests and challenges CG sequences can jar with HD-2D presentation Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy. Final Fantasy Resonance is at once a nostalgia-laced antidote for the longtime fans who have felt alienated by the recent 3D iterations turning their backs on the series' turn-based traditions as well as Square Enix giving its trademarked HD-2D style a much needed shot in the arm. While I've been enamored by this retro-modern style since its introduction in 2018's Octopath Traveler , over time it's been losing its charm, as the same presentation had been wheeled out in successive nostalgic outings, though at least Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined had the good grace to try something different . Nonetheless, its legacy of pixel-based classics like Final Fantasy 6 meant it was only a matter of time before a Final Fantasy title would receive the HD-2D treatment while also finding ways for the aesthetic to feel fresh again. Ironically, it's done that not through a brand new game but with an adaptation of mobile spin-off Final Fantasy Brave Exvius. My first Final Fantasy was Final Fantasy 8, whereafter I have played through most of the series' mainline instalments, including the 2D classics, as well as its many spin-offs, although Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius had been a blind spot. Using a Nintendo Switch 2 code provided by the publisher, I spent about 40 hours playing through Final Fantasy Resonance, completing all discovered side quests before reaching the credits. – Reviewer Alan Wen Release date: October 22, 2026 Platform(s): PC, PS5, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch Developer: In-house, Lancarse Publisher: Square Enix Square Enix reworking its mobile catalog to console may not be new, as it has done successfully with Octopath Traveler 0 , and less so with Various Daylife , but Final Fantasy Resonance is more significant as it excavates a since discontinued mobile game. The work from Square Enix Creative Studio 5 and Lancarse is even more extensive than just an act of preservation or removing the gacha elements that had been why Brave Exvius passed me by when it was available . While its story and characters remain intact, the whole presentation and experience has been overhauled to feel like a very classic yet fresh Final Fantasy adventure that stands on its own two feet. Just about everything in Final Fantasy Resonance harks back to the series' classic hallmarks , from turn-based battles with a party size of four characters to the explorable overworld of Lapis peppered with towns, dungeons, random encounters, and – of course – a story that revolves around crystals. As a knight of the kingdom of Grandshelt, your protagonist Rain finds himself setting out on a journey to find the legendary crystals before each can be destroyed by a mysterious group of elite armored warriors calling themselves the Sworn Six. There's plenty that follows a largely conventional structure – visit a new region, discover a problem the locals are having where one of the characters end up joining your party, and a dungeon that culminates in a fight with one of the Sworn Six – but it's not really a criticism when the execution of this formula is done so well. Sure, there are some familiar characterizations, from a leading man obliviously caught in a love triangle, to a feisty mechanic who's often butting heads with the sleazeball of the group, but these are fun characters to spend time with. Even the game's villains are written with pathos, while the series' recurring Espers have their own personality as you fight for the right to summon them in battle. It's all bolstered by the presentation that's a substantial level-up from past HD-2D games. While Final Fantasy Resonance does make use of voice-acting as well as having dialogue text accompanied by expressive character illustrations – the latter introduced in this year's The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales – its biggest improvement comes from the spritework, which are bigger and feature more animations than what would have been feasible for a 16-bit Final Fantasy. Another subtle yet meaningful shift seen early on is how it's not presented with the same top-down medium-wide camera but actually leverages the fact that the game is made up of 3D environments. It's not that Final Fantasy Resonance strives to be cinematic, but a simple change of the camera to a close-up, more dynamic angles during a boss encounter, or one of your party member's show-stopping Limit Bursts, does a lot to make HD-2D feel fresh again. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week It's only undermined by the occasional use of CG sequences when you're summoning Espers or Visions, the latter including manifestations of characters from the numbered Final Fantasy titles. Given how their CG sequences are taken straight from Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, I imagine they looked far more spectacular blowing up on your smartphone back in the day. I personally found these transitions at odds with the HD-2D style, and it's perhaps weirder if playing the game with English audio since the CG Visions are only voiced in Japanese. Visions are nonetheless a core component in Final Fantasy Resonance and are significantly overhauled from Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, where they were unlocked through a gacha system. sources.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Review: A nostalgic JRPG limited by its mobile origins
sources.text: Alongside Square Enix’s Pixel Remasters and other HD-2D games, Resonance isn’t an essential experience Final Fantasy Resonance doesnât really have to do anything new. This is a new adaptation of an older mobile game, Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, with the gacha system removed and progression completely reworked to befit a more standard, single-player, premium JRPG. Those are all points in its favor, and Resonance evokes the atmosphere and spirit of classic Final Fantasy, but itâs still an adaptation of that older mobile game. Resonance is set in a Final Fantasy world thatâs familiar, but not the same as the ones youâve played before (unless youâve literally played Brave Exvius). Armor-clad knights, elemental crystals, spirits, and summons. Everything about the setting, character designs, and major story beats feels cherry-picked from classic FF games that fans are nostalgic for. Thatâs not necessarily a bad thing. Final Fantasy games have a unique vibe that other long-running JRPG series just canât quite muster, and Resonance manages to evoke that atmosphere even when some numbered entries struggle to do so. On the other hand, this familiarity makes it difficult to connect with the cast when their archetypes shine through more strongly than their own personalities. I quite like the protagonist duo of Rain and Lasswell. Rain is boisterous and doesnât have the gentlemanly qualities of most knights, but is an innately talented warrior. Lasswell, meanwhile, picks up the slack to ensure his adopted brother Rain can rise in the ranks and let his talents shine. But while Lasswell is a more interesting character, he has to give way to Rain, who has unique magical abilities he doesnât understand the origin of. Aside from one major exception, most of your party members are downplayed by the plot past the chapter in which theyâre introduced. Lid is incredibly charming when you first meet her, but past that point her character moments are few and far between. Nicholâs introduction is intense and emotional, but once itâs over, it feels swept under the rug. Past that point, theyâre functional party members that give you more options in battle, and rarely more than that. The major defining feature that sets Resonance apart from other FF games is the Vision system. Youâre able to equip a Vision to each party member, and this Vision takes the form of another character from across the Final Fantasy pantheon. Upgrading Visions gives you access to more of their attacks in battle, and you can freely choose between your own characterâs pool of skills or their equipped Visionâs. Keeping a Vision equipped will enable you to level up a characterâs synergy with it, allowing you to equip abilities and skills from that Vision permanently. Itâs like a hot-swappable job system. If you feel one of your characters needs more curative skills, then you can equip them with a White Mage Vision. If you need access to Water and Thunder element attacks, then teaming up with Cloud Strife is a good idea. There are dozens of characters from different FF games available to unlock and equip as Visions â protagonists and final bosses alike â and this acts as the gameâs main hook. Swapping through Visions, increasing synergy across the cast, and building your main party members to be as capable as possible. “There are dozens of characters from different FF games available to unlock and equip as Visions â protagonists and final bosses alike â and this acts as the gameâs main hook” When collecting Visions from the various Sanctums of Light across the land, you complete a quick three-step quiz to see how well you resonate with the Vision youâre summoning, and the questions are worded so obviously that youâll probably understand what the correct answers are without ever playing the game the Vision is from. Itâs obviously an improvement over Brave Exviusâ gacha system, but these moments feel somewhat cheap, evoking nostalgia for better games. It makes sense for a mobile title, but as a premium game it falls flat. Still, Visions do a lot to spice up a battle system that is otherwise tried and tested. Itâs a traditional turn-based affair with a basic attack, each characterâs own skills, and those of your equipped Vision. You also get access to Limit Break abilities, and modifiers that allow you to build LB more quickly. The final piece of the puzzle is summonable spirits, called Espers, that act as a fifth party member for a short time in battle before unleashing a final strike on your enemies. Otherwise, youâll be using familiar Final Fantasy strategies such as using Protect and Haste to strengthen your team while staggering and damaging foes. Itâs impossible to get lost in Resonance thanks to a map which constantly shows where your next main objective is, along with any side quests youâve picked up. Side quests can offer decent rewards â including some nice upgrades for Lidâs Mecha Chocobo â but by and large theyâre pretty dull, often having you backtrack a bit through an earlier dungeon to witness a new scene or collect an item. Resonance successfully evokes the vibes and atmosphere of Final Fantasy, sure, but it doesnât live up to its inspirations. The battle system and Visions are the standout features, and even they arenât any kind of revolutionary, being broadly bettered by other HD-2D titles from Square Enix . Many of the minor qualms and complaints arenât because of any lack of talent on the behalf of the developers, I think theyâve done a great job adapting a mobile game into a premium title. But the design of its mobile origins limits this gameâs ambitions. Resonance, if it were a truly original title, couldâve been a bigger, bolder celebration of Final Fantasyâs history. As it is, it falls short of that. Final Fantasy Resonance is a fun JRPG releasing just when I personally needed a classic turn-based experience, but in a world with HD-2D rele

stories.title: Nintendo Pays Homage to Original 1998 Commercial for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time in New Remake Trailer
stories.summary: Nintendo has released a new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake trailer that pays homage to the 1998 commercial for the N64 masterpiece — and we’ve got a comparison video showing just how close it is to the original.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Nintendo Pays Homage to Original 1998 Commercial for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time in New Remake Trailer
sources.text: Nintendo has released a new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake trailer that pays homage to the 1998 commercial for the N64 masterpiece — and we’ve got a comparison video showing just how close it is to the original. Cast your mind back to 1998 and you might remember seeing a commercial for Ocarina of Time that had phrases like “A dark time is approaching,” “Willst thou run?” and “Have ye what it takes?” It’s an iconic advert that certainly got my teenage blood pumping at the time. Now, Nintendo has recreated the advert in a new trailer for the Ocarina of Time remake. It features some of the same shots and even some of the same language. “Willst thou flee? Or Fight?” the trailer asks, leaning heavily on nostalgia as Link encounters Ganondorf on his horse — just as we see him do in the original trailer. Check out a comparison in the video below. Reaction to the new trailer has been overwhelmingly positive, with warm memories of weekends spent in the glow of a CRT television successfully rekindled. “THEY DID THE TRAILER THING OMG,” one person said. “NO WAY THEY DID IT,” another added. “THY WILL PREORDER AS SOON AS THY GETS PAYDAY,” one fan joked. There is one major difference though: Nintendo’s recreation does not include the custom-recorded version of the track "Riddle of Steel / Riders of Doom" from the 1982 film Conan the Barbarian, as the original trailer did. Music rights! Marketing for the Ocarina of Time remake has ramped up, with Nintendo releasing a number of new commercials ahead of the game’s November launch. Nintendo recently released two new TV spots for Japan that, while brief, reveal a tantalizing glimpse at some never-before-seen characters, chief among them Dark Link . As Nintendo has pulled back the curtain on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake , we’ve begun to get a better understanding of how this Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive will look and feel to play. IGN has already got you covered with an extensive hands-on preview , as well as a roundup of all the changes we’ve noticed so far compared to the N64 masterpiece. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5, 2026. While you wait, check out a special episode of Nintendo Voice Chat where we dive deeper into our Zelda preview. Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake file size is over 800 times larger than the N64 original
sources.text: And it's bigger than Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom Nintendo has revealed the The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake file size, and it's mercifully not going to hog a ton of your storage space, even if it is bigger than Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. Twitter user Genki_JPN posted a photo of the download card for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2, which is now available in Japanese stores. While this doesn't reveal much beyond including some screenshots and artwork for the game, it does list the file size for the Switch 2 remake as 27GB. For context, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 shipped on a 32MB cartridge, meaning the 2026 remake is over 800 times larger than the original version in 1998. Obviously, we live in the era of 200GB Call of Duty downloads, and given that two parts of fellow 90's remake Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Rebirth are the biggest games on Switch 2 at 90.4GB and 91.5GB respectively, it's a reasonably low file size for the new Zelda remake, which is a welcome surprise. What is shocking, though, is that at 27GB, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is now the biggest mainline Zelda game of the Switch era. Breath of the Wild Nintendo Switch 2 Edition was the previous record holder at 24GB, with Tears of the Kingdom Nintendo Switch 2 Edition at only 20GB, while the Link's Awakening remake and Echoes of Wisdom both land within the 5GB range. In fact, the only Zelda game that's larger overall is Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, at 43.5GB. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake borrows one of Breath of the Wild's most immersive features Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week Scott has been freelancing for over four years across a number of different gaming publications, first appearing on GamesRadar+ in 2024. He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. He's typically rambling about Metal Gear Solid, God Hand, or any other PS2-era titles that rarely (if ever) get sequels. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake File Size Officially Confirmed
sources.text: You'll never believe how much bigger the Switch 2 game is than the Nintendo 64 original When the original Nintendo 64 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was released in 1998, the entire game fit on a 32 MB cartridge. The upcoming Nintendo Switch 2 remake does not; in fact, the updated version of the classic game is over 800 times larger. That's according to the recently revealed file size for the remake, so you should start clearing some storage space. We now know that the Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2 will take up 27 GB of storage. That's according to a photo of the game's download card in Japan, posted on X by Genki_JPN . That doesn't make the remake a big game by modern standards. The likes of Call of Duty can easily take up over 200 GB alone on consoles. It is, however, the biggest mainline Zelda game to date. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom , the most recent mainline entry in the series, takes up 24 GB on Switch 2. The only game that exceeds the size of the Ocarina of Time remake is currently Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment , the 2025 Musou spinoff, which takes up just over 43 GB. As the remake introduces a complex (if controversial ) art style and expands the game world, it makes sense that it would come with a bigger file size, though I still think it's a bit shocking that it outdoes the scale of Tears of the Kingdom Players are finally close to getting their hands on the Ocarina of Time remake. It will be released exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2 on Nov. 5, as Nintendo is one of the only companies willing to get anywhere near Grand Theft Auto 6 . In addition to the updated graphics, the game brings a number of new features , like jumping whenever you want. Wow! Polygon went hands on with the game earlier this month and came away impressed with how timeless the new version of the iconic game feels. We wrote, "Nintendo seems to have pulled it off. The remake is both incredibly impressive graphically and the game now plays better than ever. The remake evokes nostalgia for Link’s first 3D adventure while also feeling thoroughly modern." A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

sources.title: GTA 5, Red Dead Redemption 2, and More Are Being Removed from the PS Plus Game Catalog
sources.text: A bunch of games, including GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, are about to be pulled from the PlayStation Plus' catalog. Next month, players will be losing some games that have been included with their PlayStation Plus Extra or Premium subscription. These are games that are currently available through Sony's Game Pass-like catalog of titles, so you're not being stripped of any games you own or are entitled to. However, if you've been waiting to play GTA 5 or Red Dead Redemption 2, you should move quickly, as those games amongst others will be removed from the service starting on November 17. You can view the full list of games being removed below. Of course, GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 are being removed just two days before the launch of GTA 6. This is as good a time as any to catch up or revisit these titles if you're trying to build some extra hype for Rockstar's latest game. If you're not interested in an open world experience, The Talos Principle 2 is a fantastic first-person puzzle title that is absolutely worth playing before it leaves the service. If you don't manage to play these games by November 17, they will become unplayable, even if they are downloaded to your machine, unless you purchase them. So, act quickly! If you do miss these titles, PlayStation recently added a bunch of other great games available through the service , including Mafia: The Old Country and Horizon Forbidden West. sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Star Wars Zero Company review
sources.text: It took me longer than I'd like to admit to realise something obvious about Star Wars Zero Company. The fate of its eponymous crew - short of cash, betrayed by the shifting sands of circumstance in a tumultuous wider world, scrambling to just about get the job over the line - is really a lot like that of its developers at Bit Reactor. Furloughed for about a month before the game was released, those staff have clearly hustled and scrapped and fought to the last. And so Zero Company the game bears the signs of its development. In places it feels a little patched together, a little under-ready, a game that launched into the world like a roguish pilot might launch a half-repaired starfighter. The windscreen's rattling, warning lights are flashing, one particularly hirsute engineer is deeply unimpressed at the decision to take off, and nobody knows where that ominous groaning noise is coming from. But somehow she's up. And in the end that's all that counts. Zero Company is not a tidy game, then - truly, I've a list of nitpicks longer than this review - but it is also a bit of a gem. There's so much love here. At times it borders on the saccarine, some characters getting a little too wistful, moments of crewmate dialogue a little too breathy, too aww, shucks . But I've an enduring soft spot for games where you can feel the development of it as you play. And it's more than just the slightly taped-together vibes that give Zero Company that impression here. You can feel the development of this game because you can feel the thinking behind it. The many hours that years-long experts of turn-based tactics (many Bit Reactor devs have pedigree at Firaxis, developer of the modern XCOM games) have spent sat in, I'd like to imagine, a big, comfortable chair. Perhaps with their feet resting, legs crossed, up on their desk. And staring intently at the ceiling until the solution to one design problem or another presented itself. A game I imagine as being developed much the same as it's played. A nice twist, however, is in how relaxed that playing can be. Zero Company's default difficulty is on the easy side, pitched at newcomers to the turn-based tactical genre, and in turn it makes for a perfect match to the source material. Star Wars Zero Company is set in the late Clone Wars era - roughly parallel to Episode 3, in other words - which also happens to be the prime kids TV era. This is the time when Obi Wan Kenobi was a cool action figure warrior-general with big shoulder pads and there were lots of Trooper dudes with names like Rex diving around shooting their lasers. It's also the period that plays home to Andor, the gloriously realised political melodrama about revolution, solidarity, and the banality of evil under fascism, perched right at the opposite end of the Star Wars Seriousness Spectrum. And so Zero Company has these two, ostensibly opposing threads running through it, tasking it with somehow tying together light entertainment and timely introspection. And somehow, it does it quite well. The default difficulty is part of the reason why (though there are hard and ironman-like modes for the true tacticos and sickos out there, of course). There's a novelty to angling a game in this genre - a genre more often associated with those iron men - at the casual crowd, in aiming for breeziness and satisfaction first. This is my first time enjoying one of these games as a good old-fashioned romp, where there might be the occasional grabbing of a hat beneath the closing door but, broadly speaking, you will find yourself playing as the good guys who ultimately always come out on top. That pairs nicely with Zero Company's take on telling a story. Rather than the XCOM approach of an aggressively replayable campaign with a feather-light narrative layer, Zero Company has a proper beginning-middle-end story. This is where the Andor side of things comes in. Zero Company is far from that level of writing and execution, unfortunately, and perhaps expectedly. It relays its themes broadly and a little clunkily, falling into familiar video game traps that so often feel unavoidable because of the way the game itself is structured. Characters, for instance, often need to deliver entire backstories in a couple of throwaway lines - lines which most players might never hear because they didn't opt to talk to the right static NPC between the right missions. Or which they might hear a variation of multiple times because they talked to them at every opportunity, and developers need to make sure those skip-lots-of-conversations players get their required minimum exposition to know what's going on. There's also a lot of overly-breathy voice work - Jae, who has a moderately interesting background as a kind of ore-baron nepo baby who wants to do good, is a particular culprit of the kind of over-earnestness that can jar just a little. The truth is a lot of Star Wars media is always going to struggle to execute its themes with the sophistication we now know to be possible, post-Andor. But what helps Zero Company is that those themes are at least there , and more than that, they're both fully understood and delivered with heartfelt sincerity. There's a wonderful transition, which I'll try not to spoil, where this crew's story shifts from underdog adventure-romp (that's the third of Star Wars' three pillars accounted for: original trilogy ruffian-camp), through Clone Wars action melodrama, and out the other side into something about bigger ideas. I only wish it had gone on for a little longer after that point - you'll know it when you play it - to give that final part a bit more time to breathe. All that said, I expect most people coming to Zero Company are coming because you can conveniently shorten it to ZCOM. This is a tactics game from tactics virtuosos, ultimately, and in the playing is where it really shows. The big twist for XCOM fans is the removal of the two-action limit. Here you get three, though rather than that simply feeli

sources.title: We've had two great Star Wars games this year, probably because Lucasfilm Games says it's now "more flexible" about who it takes pitches from
sources.text: "We're exploring all kinds of things, large and small." This year has seen two highly-rated and beloved Star Wars games in the XCOM-like Zero Company , and the Burnout-like Galactic Racer . And both were made by independent studios rather than much bigger companies, which have typically taken on Star Wars games in recent years, such as Ubisoft with Star Wars Outlaws and EA with Star Wars Battlefront. The change, it turns out, was intentional. Lucasfilm Games bigwig Douglas Reilly told The Game Business that the Star Wars franchise stewards are now much more open about who to give the license to. "We're obviously a licensing business," Reilly explained, "so we're not the publishers any more of products. Our goal is to try and find a publishing partner and a developer or a publisher and a developer. I think we've tried to be more flexible about who we're willing to take pitches from. Good ideas can come from a lot of different places." This is a fairly recent change in Lucasfilm Games' strategy. The license holder was previously happy to sell a single publisher exclusive rights to Star Wars games, which previously was EA. That approach has often been criticised for limiting the creative output, be it in the number of games released or genres that get chosen. That dearth is something Star Wars fans truly felt when EA had exclusive rights to Star Wars, but this new approach allows for a much more varied pool of games and more frequent releases. To that end, Reilly revealed there is no particular tier of publisher that Lucasfilm Games targets, saying, "There are some hurdles; we have a high quality bar and we want to make sure they're excellent experiences. And that means typically you work with more experienced teams than new teams." However, that doesn't mean you "necessarily [have to] be a top-five publisher to make a great Star Wars game". Reilly also teased what we can expect from Star Wars games in the future. "We're exploring all kinds of things, large and small," he said, "with partners that I think are going to continue to surprise folks who are like, 'Oh, they're doing a thing with them. That might be interesting to see how that turns out.'" The number of currently announced Star Wars games remains small. Outside of Quantic Dream's long-in-development Star Wars Eclipse , the only other game that's understood to be in the works is the third game in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi series . Former Mass Effect and Knights of the Old Republic lead Casey Hudson is currently working on a follow-up, Fate of the Old Republic , as Saber Interactive continues to insist the Knights of the Old Republic Remake remains in development .

sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: Lucasfilm wants to do more Star Wars games like Zero Company and Galactic Racer: 'We’ve tried to be more flexible about who we’re willing to take pitches from'
sources.text: Not every Star Wars game has to be a big-budget blockbuster to be successful. We've had two Star Wars games in 2026, both of them quite good and neither of them quite what you might expect from the Star Wars mould: Zero Company , an XCOM-style tactics game, and Galactic Racer , an arcade racing game but Star Wars. And the success of those games means we may see more like them—which is to say, more offbeat Star Wars games from smaller-scale studios—in the future. Both Zero Company and Galactic Racer were developed by independent studios—Bit Reactor and Fuse Games, respectively—and that "very much is part of the strategy," Lucasfilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly told The Game Business . "Obviously, huge triple-A games like Battlefront are always going to be an essential part of the strategy," Reilly said. "But one of the great things about Star Wars is it has all kinds of other opportunities to tell stories in different genres. "The goal has been to find the best partner who makes that experience come alive inside the galaxy far, far away. And it doesn’t have to always be triple-A, sometimes it can be double-A, and it’s really about the experience that we’re delivering and the fantasy we’re fulfilling." That's a real shift in Disney's approach to making Star Wars games. Disney acquired Lucasfilm in 2012 and shuttered its games division the following year; not long after that, it signed a 10-year deal with Electronic Arts , granting it exclusive rights to make Star Wars games. That deal was not especially fruitful, and Ubisoft 's big-budget Star Wars Outlaws , announced in the waning years of the EA deal, didn't exactly set the world on fire either. Disney also resurrected Lucasfilm Games in 2021, making it "the official identity for all gaming titles from Lucasfilm"—which, as the sizzle reel made clear, meant Star Wars games—and it's "tried to be more flexible about who we’re willing to take pitches from," Reilly said. "Good ideas can come from a lot of different places. You don’t have to necessarily be a top five publisher to make a great Star Wars game. There are some hurdles. We have a high quality bar, and that means typically we work with more experienced teams than ones with no track record. But we’re exploring all kinds of things, large and small, with partners that are going to surprise folks." From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews Of course, there are plenty of familiar-looking Star Wars games in the trench too: Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic , a new addition to the Knights of the Old Republic series, was announced at The Game Awards in 2025, the third and supposedly last Star Wars Jedi game is in development, Quantic Dream is still plugging away on Star Wars: Eclipse, despite recent reports of struggles , and yes, that KOTOR remake is, somehow, still happening . 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill. sources.title: Red Dead Redemption e Bully quase não existiram, revela cofundador da Rockstar
sources.text: Dificuldades de desenvolvimento deixaram em risco dois grandes títulos do estúdio. Houser comenta que desenvolver jogos AAA já é um desafio por si só e, no caso de novas franquias, as dificuldades são ainda maiores. Por isso, a equipe responsável acaba se surpreendendo mais quando o título é finalmente lançado do que quando o projeto é cancelado. Ele revela que Red Dead Redemption enfrentou muitos momentos decisivos, mas conseguiu superar os obstáculos graças às “ pessoas fundamentais da equipe, que eram realmente fortes, mantiveram o foco no que estavam tentando fazer e resolveram os problemas ”. O principal deles, segundo Houser era “ desvendar o que havia de interessante em um jogo de mundo aberto sobre caubóis ”. Com o sucesso do título, que garantiu uma sequência maior e melhor em 2018, é um tanto “óbvio” perceber o que há de interessante no jogo, olhando em retrospecto. “ Mas, enquanto tudo acontecia, não havia nada além de espaços vazios que precisaram preencher aos poucos ”, acrescenta Houser.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: GTA 6 is so detailed no single Rockstar employee knows it all - which is how we got shrinking horse testicles in Red Dead Redemption 2
sources.text: Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous animated horse testicles , which are realistic enough to contract in cold weather and expand again in the warmth, were apparently not a feature mandated by Rockstar. As iconic as they've become - a symbol of extraordinary detail in the game - they didn't originate from a list of features that needed to be added to the game. The horse testicles were instead the unexpected work of one person, or a group of people, autonomously working on the Cowboy epic. Journalist Jason Schreier heard this anecdote from Rockstar head of development Aaron Garbut while visiting Rockstar North to write an expansive report for Bloomberg about the making of GTA 6 . "Garbut actually brought this up," Schreier said in a video on YouTube . "[The horse testicles were] not something that was on some big list of features to make; it was not something that an art director told an artist, 'Alright, we've got to get those horse testicles in here - better put in nights and weekends so you can get these horse testicles in here.' "That was something that people, or a person on their own, autonomously decided, 'OK, I'm going to do this because I think it's a really cool detail and I have enough time to work on it." We're checking the veracity of this anecdote with Rockstar, by the way. And that anecdote is important because it relates to another thing Schreier was told by Garbut, which was that no one person at Rockstar knows everything that's in GTA 6 because it's too big and detailed to do that. "There's no one person that has this whole thing in their head," Garbut apparently said. That, coupled with the fact that developers apparently have "autonomy to put in things that are cool", Schreier said, means there could be another unexpected feature like horse testicles in GTA 6. And given the nudity-related GTA 6 video leaks we've already had , perhaps the features aren't that far removed. Schreier's video revealed a few other tidbits of information learnt on his trip to Rockstar. He was told that roads in GTA 6 are "significantly narrower" than in GTA 5 , apparently, so players feel the effects of traffic more - a detail that relates to the increased levels of realism in GTA 6 . He also heard how some artists had been working on GTA 6 for 11 years, and whereas there were "five of six" people in GTA 5's art production team, there were - or are - 65 people in GTA 6's art production team. Note that Rockstar, as a company, has roughly doubled in size since the release of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2 , growing from 2,441 employees to 4,711 across 12 offices. There's also some information about the origins of the contextual 'hold left trigger' interaction system introduced in Red Dead Redemption 2, which again, apparently came from someone autonomously working on the game - Phil Hooker (now director of technology) - rather than from one of the game's creative leads. Also, many experiments were apparently done to find a replacement for GTA's radial menu but in the end, the team reverted back to it. Grand Theft Auto 6 is, of course, releasing a month from now on 19th November. The road to launch has been bumpy, however, with Rockstar North currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland over the alleged unjust firings of 31 employees, and with a series of gameplay footage leaks exposing GTA 6 in ways that are outside of Rockstar's control.

sources.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer boss on DLC and the ‘remarkable’ rise of Biddy Blas
sources.text: Fuse Games CEO Matt Webster chats about what’s next for the hit racing game Fuse Games CEO Matt Webster has sat down with VGC for an in-depth chat about Star Wars: Galactic Racer’s success, the future of the game, and the viral stardom of Biddy Blas. Speaking with VGC following the game’s hugely positive reviews and player sentiment, Webster chats about what players should expect next from the game, and what the team is prioritizing post-launch. Webster also tells VGC about some of the early days of working with Lucasfilm Games. You can watch the complete conversation below. A chat about Star Wars: Galactic Racer wouldn’t be complete without some words for Biddy Blas, a side character in the game that has shot to viral stardom following clips on social media being viewed millions of times. We asked Webster what he thought of the game’s unlikely main character. “It’s remarkable, isn’t it?,” Webster said. “What is quite funny is that we were talking about the Biddy Base fan club at the preview event because everyone has their favorites and then we kind of forgot about him a little bit. I knew there was a few characters in this game that people were really going to connect with. Hibi being one of them, Biddy being the other. “That just shows you how much this galaxy is loved, because it can support characters like that then people just take it and run with it. And it’s unexpected alien creatures and the characterizations that we’ve learned and we worked so closely with Lucasfilm Games on. Bringing them to life and you call them a rogue’s gallery, that’s exactly how we talked about it. This group of races that go around with you on the racing circuit and you get to learn a little bit more about them.
